title: 07 — Azure Functions for .NET Developers
html:
07 — Azure Functions for .NET Developers

⚠️ The most important thing in this file: the in-process model is retired on 10 November 2026. .NET 8 support ends the same day. Every .NET Functions app must be on the isolated worker model, targeting .NET 10 (supported to Nov 2028) or .NET 8 isolated as a short bridge. The C# in-process model is also not supported at all on the Flex Consumption plan.

1. In-process vs isolated worker

In-process (retired 10 Nov 2026) Isolated worker ✅
Runs Inside the Functions host process A separate process the host talks to over gRPC
.NET versions Only the host's version Any supported .NET, including preview and non-LTS
DI, middleware, config Constrained by the host Full Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting — your own Program.cs, middleware pipeline, DI
Dependency conflicts ⚠️ Your assemblies collide with the host's Isolated — no conflicts
Cold start Slightly faster Marginally slower (a second process)
Flex Consumption ❌ Not supported ✅ Required

Migration is not optional. The practical steps:

- <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>
- <AzureFunctionsVersion>v4</AzureFunctionsVersion>
+ <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
+ <AzureFunctionsVersion>v4</AzureFunctionsVersion>
+ <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>

- Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Functions                     (package)
+ Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker
+ Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker.Sdk
+ Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker.Extensions.*   (per binding)
In-process API Isolated equivalent
[FunctionName("X")] [Function("X")]
ILogger injected as a parameter ILogger<T> from constructor DI, or FunctionContext.GetLogger()
HttpRequest / IActionResult HttpRequestData / HttpResponseData (or ASP.NET Core integration — see §3)
FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME=dotnet dotnet-isolated ⚠️ Change this app setting or the app won't start
Startup via FunctionsStartup Your own Program.cs with HostApplicationBuilder

2. Anatomy of an isolated-worker app

// Program.cs — this is a normal .NET host; everything you know applies
var builder = FunctionsApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.ConfigureFunctionsWebApplication();          // ASP.NET Core integration for HTTP triggers

builder.Services
    .AddApplicationInsightsTelemetryWorkerService()
    .ConfigureFunctionsApplicationInsights();

builder.Services.AddDbContextPool<AppDbContext>(o =>
    o.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Sql")));

builder.Services.AddAzureClients(clients =>
{
    clients.UseCredential(new DefaultAzureCredential());
    clients.AddBlobServiceClient(new Uri(builder.Configuration["StorageUri"]!));
});

builder.Services.AddOptions<PricingOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection("Pricing"))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();

builder.UseMiddleware<ExceptionHandlingMiddleware>();   // your own middleware pipeline

builder.Build().Run();

// A function: a class with constructor DI, exactly like any other service
public sealed class TradeFunctions(
    ITradeService trades,
    ILogger<TradeFunctions> logger)
{
    [Function(nameof(ProcessTrade))]
    public async Task ProcessTrade(
        [ServiceBusTrigger("trades", Connection = "ServiceBusConnection")]
        ServiceBusReceivedMessage message,
        ServiceBusMessageActions actions,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var trade = message.Body.ToObjectFromJson<TradeMessage>();

        using var scope = logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object>
        {
            ["MessageId"] = message.MessageId,
            ["CorrelationId"] = message.CorrelationId ?? "none",
        });

        try
        {
            await trades.ProcessAsync(trade, cancellationToken);
            await actions.CompleteMessageAsync(message, cancellationToken);
        }
        catch (ValidationException ex)                 // permanent — retrying cannot help
        {
            logger.LogWarning(ex, "Invalid trade message {MessageId}", message.MessageId);
            await actions.DeadLetterMessageAsync(message, cancellationToken,
                deadLetterReason: "ValidationFailed", deadLetterErrorDescription: ex.Message);
        }
        // transient exceptions: let them bubble → the host abandons → Service Bus redelivers
    }
}

3. Triggers and bindings

One trigger per function (what starts it) plus zero or more input/output bindings (declarative I/O).

Trigger Fires on Notes
HTTP A request AuthorizationLevel.Function (key) / Anonymous (put Entra auth in front)
Timer A CRON schedule ⚠️ 6 fields ({second} {minute} {hour} {day} {month} {day-of-week}) — not 5
Service Bus Queue/topic message ⭐ The workhorse. Sessions supported for ordering
Storage Queue Queue message Simpler and cheaper than Service Bus; fewer guarantees
Blob Blob created/updated ⚠️ Polling-based and can be minutes late on Consumption. Use Event Grid–based blob triggers for low latency
Event Hub Stream events Batched; checkpointing per partition
Event Grid Resource/custom events Push-based, near-real-time
Cosmos DB Change feed Great for materialised views
Durable Orchestration §6 
// HTTP with the ASP.NET Core integration (from ConfigureFunctionsWebApplication)
[Function("GetPortfolio")]
public async Task<IResult> GetPortfolio(
    [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "get", Route = "portfolios/{id:guid}")]
    HttpRequest request,
    Guid id,
    CancellationToken ct)
{
    var portfolio = await service.GetAsync(id, ct);
    return portfolio is null ? Results.NotFound() : Results.Ok(portfolio);
}

// Timer — 6 fields. This is 02:00 every weekday, UTC unless WEBSITE_TIME_ZONE is set.
[Function("NightlyReconciliation")]
public async Task Run([TimerTrigger("0 0 2 * * 1-5")] TimerInfo timer, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (timer.IsPastDue) logger.LogWarning("Timer is past due — the host may have been down");
    await reconciliation.RunAsync(ct);
}

// Output binding — declarative, no client code
[Function("EnqueueReport")]
[ServiceBusOutput("reports", Connection = "ServiceBusConnection")]
public async Task<string> EnqueueReport(
    [HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post")] HttpRequest request, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var command = await request.ReadFromJsonAsync<GenerateReport>(ct);
    return JsonSerializer.Serialize(command);        // the return value is written to the queue
}

3.1 Identity-based connections (no connection strings)

// Instead of  "ServiceBusConnection": "Endpoint=sb://...;SharedAccessKey=..."
// use the __fullyQualifiedNamespace convention and a managed identity:
{
  "ServiceBusConnection__fullyQualifiedNamespace": "sb-shop-prod.servicebus.windows.net",
  "AzureWebJobsStorage__accountName": "stshopprod",
  "StorageConnection__serviceUri": "https://stshopprod.blob.core.windows.net"
}

Then grant the function app's managed identity Azure Service Bus Data Receiver, Storage Blob Data Owner, and — for AzureWebJobsStorage — also Storage Queue Data Contributor and Storage Table Data Contributor 🔄.

⚠️ AzureWebJobsStorage is mandatory. The runtime uses it for triggers, leases, checkpoints, and the timer schedule. If it's misconfigured, functions silently never fire — no error, no logs, nothing. This is the single most common "my function doesn't run" cause.

4. Hosting plans

Plan Scale to zero Cold start VNet Max duration 🔄 Cost model
Consumption ✅ Yes (seconds) Limited 5 min default / 10 max Per execution + GB-s. Free grant
Flex Consumption ⭐ ✅ Reduced (always-ready instances) ✅ Full Configurable, longer Per execution + provisioned concurrency
Premium (EP) ❌ (min 1) ~None (pre-warmed) ✅ Full Unlimited Per vCPU/GB-hour — expensive at idle
Dedicated (App Service plan) ❌ None with Always On ✅ Unlimited The plan you already pay for
Container Apps ✅ Configurable ✅ Unlimited Per replica

🔄 Important current facts:

  • Linux Consumption is being retired — the migration path is Flex Consumption.
  • .NET 10 on Linux requires Flex Consumption, not classic Consumption.
  • Flex Consumption supports always-ready instances (a floor of warm instances) plus per-instance concurrency control — which largely solves the cold-start objection without Premium's cost.

Choosing:

Spiky/unpredictable, cost-sensitive, tolerant of some cold start  →  Flex Consumption ⭐
Latency-critical, needs VNet + no cold start, steady load          →  Premium (EP1+)
Already paying for an App Service plan with spare capacity         →  Dedicated
Containerised, KEDA scaling, sharing an environment with services  →  Container Apps

4.1 Cold start — what actually causes it and what helps

Causes: allocating an instance, downloading and extracting the package, starting the host, starting the .NET worker process, JIT, and your own startup work (DI graph, EF model, config providers).

Mitigation Effect
Always-ready / pre-warmed instances (Flex, Premium) Removes it for the baseline
WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE=1 Faster, atomic package mount
Trim dependencies Every assembly costs load time
ReadyToRun (<PublishReadyToRun>true</PublishReadyToRun>) Cuts JIT time meaningfully
Lazy-init expensive things Don't build an EF model or warm a cache for a function that doesn't need it
Static/singleton clients ⭐ See §5 — a new HttpClient or SqlConnection per invocation is the biggest self-inflicted cost

5. ⚠️ The connection-exhaustion trap

Functions scale to hundreds of instances, each with its own process. Anything created per invocation is multiplied by (instances × concurrency).

// ❌ Catastrophic at scale: 200 instances × 100 concurrent = 20,000 sockets → SNAT exhaustion
[Function("BadExample")]
public async Task Run([QueueTrigger("work")] string message)
{
    using var http = new HttpClient();                  // new sockets every time
    using var conn = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
    ...
}

// ✔ Inject singletons; the host reuses them across invocations on that instance
public sealed class GoodExample(IHttpClientFactory httpFactory, AppDbContext db)
{
    [Function("GoodExample")]
    public async Task Run([QueueTrigger("work")] string message, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var client = httpFactory.CreateClient("pricing");
        ...
    }
}

Also control concurrency, or a burst of messages will overwhelm your database:

// host.json
{
  "version": "2.0",
  "extensions": {
    "serviceBus": {
      "maxConcurrentCalls": 16,              // per instance
      "maxAutoLockRenewalDuration": "00:05:00",
      "prefetchCount": 0
    },
    "queues": { "batchSize": 16, "maxDequeueCount": 5, "newBatchThreshold": 8 }
  },
  "functionTimeout": "00:10:00",
  "logging": {
    "applicationInsights": {
      "samplingSettings": { "isEnabled": true, "maxTelemetryItemsPerSecond": 20 }
    }
  }
}

💡 On Consumption/Flex you can also cap total scale with functionAppScaleLimit — essential when the downstream (a database, a partner API) can't take unbounded parallelism. A Function app scaling to 200 instances against a 100-connection SQL pool is a self-inflicted outage.

6. Durable Functions

For stateful workflows: orchestration, fan-out/fan-in, human approval, long-running jobs with checkpointing.

[Function(nameof(RebalanceOrchestrator))]
public static async Task<RebalanceResult> RebalanceOrchestrator(
    [OrchestrationTrigger] TaskOrchestrationContext context)
{
    var request = context.GetInput<RebalanceRequest>()!;

    // Fan out — all run in parallel across instances
    var tasks = request.PortfolioIds
        .Select(id => context.CallActivityAsync<PortfolioResult>(nameof(CalculateOverlap), id))
        .ToList();

    var results = await Task.WhenAll(tasks);            // fan in

    // Durable timer + external event: wait up to 24h for human approval
    using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
    var approval = context.WaitForExternalEvent<bool>("Approval");
    var timeout  = context.CreateTimer(context.CurrentUtcDateTime.AddHours(24), cts.Token);

    if (approval == await Task.WhenAny(approval, timeout))
    {
        cts.Cancel();
        if (approval.Result)
            await context.CallActivityAsync(nameof(SubmitTrades), results);
    }
    else
    {
        await context.CallActivityAsync(nameof(NotifyTimeout), request.RequestId);
    }

    return new RebalanceResult(results);
}

⚠️ Orchestrator code must be deterministic. It is replayed from the event-source history on every resumption, so:

❌ Never in an orchestrator ✅ Instead
DateTime.UtcNow context.CurrentUtcDateTime
Guid.NewGuid() context.NewGuid()
Random, Task.Delay context.CreateTimer(...)
HTTP calls, database access, file I/O Put them in an activity function
Task.Run, ConfigureAwait(false), non-durable async Only await durable APIs
Environment variables that change Pass values in as input

Patterns: function chaining, fan-out/fan-in, async HTTP API (202 + status endpoint), monitor (polling with a durable timer), human interaction (external events), and the saga/compensation pattern for distributed transactions.

Cost note: every orchestration step writes to the durable store (Azure Storage tables/queues by default), so a chatty orchestration with thousands of tiny activities generates a lot of storage transactions. Batch where you can, and consider the Netherite or MSSQL backends for high throughput 🔄.

7. Reliability, retries, and idempotency

Delivery is at-least-once. Your functions must be idempotent. A message can be delivered twice because of a lock expiry, a host restart mid-processing, or a retry.

// Idempotency via a dedupe table, in the SAME transaction as the effect
public async Task HandleAsync(TradeApproved message, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
    try
    {
        db.ProcessedMessages.Add(new ProcessedMessage(message.MessageId, clock.GetUtcNow()));
        await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);          // UNIQUE constraint on MessageId
    }
    catch (DbUpdateException ex) when (ex.IsUniqueViolation())
    {
        logger.LogInformation("Message {Id} already processed; skipping", message.MessageId);
        return;
    }
    await ApplyEffectAsync(message, ct);
    await tx.CommitAsync(ct);
}

Retry configuration (isolated worker):

[Function("ProcessTrade")]
[ExponentialBackoffRetry(maxRetryCount: 5,
    minimumInterval: "00:00:02", maximumInterval: "00:05:00")]
public async Task Run([ServiceBusTrigger("trades")] ServiceBusReceivedMessage message) { ... }

⚠️ Function-level retries and Service Bus delivery counts interact confusingly. Function retries happen within one delivery, so the Service Bus maxDeliveryCount (and therefore dead-lettering) only advances after the retries are exhausted and the message is abandoned. 💡 For Service Bus, prefer letting the broker handle retry and dead-lettering — set maxDeliveryCount and don't add function-level retries on top, or you multiply the attempts.

Timer functions: ⚠️ IsPastDue tells you the trigger fired late (the host was down). Also note timers use a storage lease for singleton behaviour, so only one instance runs them — but that lease lives in AzureWebJobsStorage, which is one more reason it must be correct.

8. Local development and testing

func start                                     # Azure Functions Core Tools
func azure functionapp publish func-shop-prod  # (prefer CI/CD over this)

// local.settings.json  — ⚠️ NEVER commit this; it's git-ignored by the template for a reason
{
  "IsEncrypted": false,
  "Values": {
    "AzureWebJobsStorage": "UseDevelopmentStorage=true",     // Azurite emulator
    "FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME": "dotnet-isolated",
    "ServiceBusConnection__fullyQualifiedNamespace": "sb-shop-dev.servicebus.windows.net"
  }
}

Testing: because functions in the isolated model are ordinary classes with constructor injection, test the service they call, not the function. The function should be a thin adapter: bind input → call a service → map the result.

[Fact]
public async Task ProcessAsync_WithDuplicateMessage_DoesNotApplyEffectTwice()
{
    // Test the SERVICE. The function attribute adds nothing worth testing.
    await service.ProcessAsync(message, default);
    await service.ProcessAsync(message, default);
    repository.Received(1).Save(Arg.Any<Trade>());
}

Use Azurite for Storage and Testcontainers for SQL/Service Bus emulation in integration tests 🔄.

9. Security

  • Managed identity + identity-based connections for every binding (§3.1) — no connection strings.
  • HTTP triggers: AuthorizationLevel.Function uses a shared key in a header/query string — acceptable for service-to-service, not for user-facing auth. For user auth, put Entra ID in front (App Service Authentication / Easy Auth) or validate a JWT in middleware.
  • Never AuthorizationLevel.Anonymous on anything that mutates state without another auth mechanism.
  • Network: private endpoints for the storage account and dependencies; VNet integration on Flex/Premium; disable public network access where possible.
  • Secrets: Key Vault references in app settings, same as App Service.
  • ⚠️ Function keys are not an authorisation system. They identify a caller, not a user, and they're often shared and rarely rotated.

10. Monitoring

What Where
Invocations, success/failure, duration Application Insights → Performance / Failures
Live Metrics Real-time during a deploy or an incident
Scale-out behaviour FunctionExecutionCount, instance count metrics
Queue depth / consumer lag ⭐ The primary health signal for queue-triggered functions
Cold starts Look at duration distribution — a bimodal histogram is cold vs warm 
// Failures by function over the last 24h
requests
| where timestamp > ago(24h)
| summarize total = count(), failed = countif(success == false) by operation_Name
| extend failureRate = round(100.0 * failed / total, 2)
| order by failed desc

// p95 duration trend per function
requests
| where timestamp > ago(7d)
| summarize p95 = percentile(duration, 95) by bin(timestamp, 1h), operation_Name
| render timechart

💡 Alert on the age of the oldest unprocessed message, not just the queue depth — it catches a stalled consumer even at low volume.

⚠️ Application Insights sampling is on by default in Functions. Under high volume you will lose telemetry. Configure samplingSettings deliberately in host.json and exclude the request/exception types you must never lose.

11. When NOT to use Functions

Situation Better option
A long-running, steady, CPU-bound workload App Service / Container Apps — Consumption billing gets expensive and you fight timeouts
Strict sub-100ms latency with no tolerance for cold start App Service, or Premium with pre-warmed instances
A complex web API with lots of shared middleware and routing ASP.NET Core on App Service
Something needing very long execution (hours) Durable Functions, Container Apps jobs, or a worker service
Heavy state shared across invocations Anything with a persistent process

💡 The good fits: event processing, scheduled jobs, glue between services, webhook receivers, file-arrival processing, and bursty asynchronous work.

12. Checklist

  • Isolated worker model on .NET 10 (or .NET 8 isolated as a bridge) — in-process retires 10 Nov 2026
  • FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME = dotnet-isolated
  • Hosting plan chosen deliberately; Flex Consumption for Linux/scale-to-zero
  • AzureWebJobsStorage configured correctly (identity-based where possible) — verify triggers actually fire
  • Managed identity + identity-based connections; no connection strings with keys
  • Clients (HttpClient, DbContext, SDK clients) injected as singletons, never created per invocation
  • Concurrency limits in host.json and a scale limit, matched to downstream capacity
  • Idempotent handlers — at-least-once delivery is guaranteed
  • Retry strategy chosen once (broker-level for Service Bus), not doubled up
  • Dead-letter handling with alerting on DLQ depth
  • functionTimeout set explicitly; long work moved to Durable or a worker
  • Orchestrators deterministic — no clock, no GUIDs, no I/O
  • Application Insights connected; sampling configured deliberately
  • Alerts on failure rate, queue depth, and oldest-message age
  • HTTP triggers not anonymous unless deliberately public; real auth in front for user-facing endpoints

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • In-process vs isolated worker? Isolated runs your code in a separate process with full DI, middleware and any .NET version, and no dependency conflicts with the host. In-process is retired on 10 November 2026 and isn't supported on Flex Consumption at all.
  • Why does my function scale to 200 instances and kill the database? Each instance opens its own connections; you need maxConcurrentCalls plus a scale limit matched to downstream capacity — and singleton clients rather than per-invocation ones.
  • How do you make a queue-triggered function safe? At-least-once delivery means idempotency: a dedupe key committed in the same transaction as the effect, or a naturally idempotent operation.
  • Consumption vs Premium vs Flex? Scale-to-zero with cold start / always warm with VNet at higher cost / scale-to-zero with always-ready instances and full VNet — Flex is the modern default for Linux.
  • Why isn't my function triggering at all? Nine times out of ten, AzureWebJobsStorage — the runtime uses it for leases and triggers, and a misconfiguration fails silently.
  • What can't you do in a Durable orchestrator? Anything non-deterministic — the code is replayed from history, so clocks, GUIDs, randomness and I/O must come from the context or an activity.

Sources: Guide for running C# Functions in an isolated worker process — Microsoft Learn · Differences between in-process and isolated worker · Flex Consumption plan hosting · Azure Functions runtime versions · Upgrading Azure Functions to .NET 10 · Linux Consumption migration paths
